messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

John is a 30-year-old North American male who works as a carpenter and is married. The traumatic event that has profoundly affected him occurred about six months ago when he witnessed his friend’s brutal attack at the construction site where they both worked. John had been standing near a pile of lumber, hammer in hand, when he heard the sudden commotion nearby. His eyes immediately locked onto the sight of blood and visible injuries as another worker was violently assaulted by multiple assailants. The incident left him shaken to his core. Since then, John’s life has been marked by distressing triggers that often arise unexpectedly. The mere taste of a specific snack he had eaten just before witnessing the attack can transport him back to that moment with startling clarity. He finds himself consumed by vivid and full sensory reliving of the event, so real it feels as if he is there again, unable to escape the horror. This type of intrusive memory has left John struggling to put what happened into words, leading to a profound sense of isolation. John’s maladaptive strategies have become habitual responses to this distress. He often overeats, using food as a way to numb his emotions and distract himself from the trauma. On other occasions, he deliberately tries to dissociate or blank out entirely when confronted with triggers like physical touch or seeing visible injuries on others. These behaviors are driven by his fear that any reminder of the event could reignite the overwhelming sensations he experienced. John has come to believe that his life has been irrevocably destroyed by this trauma, and he can’t rely on himself anymore. He feels permanently changed for the worse, a sentiment that only deepens when intrusive memories surface unexpectedly. The more he experiences these traumatic memories, the more intensely he engages in maladaptive strategies like overeating or dissociation to cope. The cycle has become self-reinforcing: every time John is triggered by a taste or touch, it sends him spiraling into intense distress. This triggers his memory, which feels as real and visceral as if the event were happening again, further reinforcing his negative appraisals about himself and life. He believes that he can no longer trust his own reactions or coping mechanisms, leading to more avoidance behaviors and heightened sensitivity to triggers. At work, John finds it increasingly difficult to focus on his tasks. The sight of blood on a job site where he once felt confident now causes him severe anxiety, often leaving him unable to continue working effectively. This has strained his relationship with colleagues and supervisors, who have noticed his growing disengagement and avoidance behaviors. John’s marriage is also affected; he has become distant from his wife, spending more time alone or in isolation when triggers arise. The fear of being overwhelmed by memories drives much of this behavior, but it has left a significant gap between them that neither can ignore. It was the culmination of these issues—his inability to work effectively, the strain on his marriage, and an increasingly isolated life—that finally pushed John to seek help. He is most afraid of never being able to reclaim his former self or feel safe again. Yet, he also harbors a glimmer of hope that through therapy, he might find ways to manage his symptoms and start rebuilding his sense of self and security.
